Lessons.Title: Arrange Objects Into Arrays
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: build arrays with physical objects and describe an array as equal-size rows and equal-size columns, relating that geometry to equal groups. First-edition 2021 Grade 3 Unit 1 Lesson 16; the text and diagrams below are independently authored by Edulytics. This is not an arithmetic-only lesson.

Warm-up — Notice and Wonder: Eggs (10 minutes). The source shows an open carton with 12 eggs. With a partner, discuss what you observe and ask; teacher highlights equal rows/columns and how the same objects may be regrouped. The original egg photograph is source media and is NOT embedded or represented as verified Edulytics artwork.

Activity 1 — Compare Equal Groups and Arrays (15 minutes). Compare four circles containing five dots each (20 in total) with 20 dots arranged in a rectangular array. Objects remain the same total but the representation changes: an array has equally populated rows and columns. Students examine Noah's incorrect claim that only separate circles, not arrays, have equal groups. Both an array row and an array column can be an equal group; teacher assesses the argument and discussion, not a single integer answer.

Activity 2 — Arrange Into Arrays (20 minutes). The teacher supplies at least 60 connecting cubes per pair. Students first arrange six groups of five (30 cubes) into an array and explain the same equal-group structure. They then use all 20 cubes to build and draw several rectangular arrays and repeat with all 24 cubes. For 20, valid examples include 4 by 5 and 2 by 10. For 24, valid examples include 4 by 6 and 3 by 8. These are first-party illustrative possibilities: the source does NOT require finding every possible factor pair, so grading an exhaustive list would misalign the lesson.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes). Ask children to describe how they arranged the objects and why every row contains the same amount and every column also contains the same amount. Students compare models and reflect on how equal groups are preserved under rearrangement. Partner explanations, original cube constructions and drawings are teacher-observed.

Cool-down (5 minutes). The publisher's original educator-gated Array Arrangement prompt was not read or copied. An independently authored Edulytics equivalent asks learners to make two different arrays using 24 counters, sketch them and explain the row/column groupings. Correct multiplication totals alone cannot establish this source target: this first-party Cool-down is human-reviewed, not automatically passed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Array
KeyConcepts.Definition: A regular arrangement of objects into rows and columns.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every row contains the same number of objects, and every column contains the same number of objects.
KeyConcepts.Example: Six rows of five cubes form an array of 30 objects.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal-group interpretation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Array rows or columns may each be read as equal-sized groups.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Distinguish an arrangement of dots in separate circles from an equivalent rectangular layout without changing the total.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four groups of five and a 4-by-5 array each represent 20 objects.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple valid arrays
KeyConcepts.Definition: The same whole-number total can sometimes be arranged into different rectangular arrays.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For each candidate arrangement, verify that all available cubes are used and row lengths are equal.
KeyConcepts.Example: Twenty cubes may form a 4-by-5 or 2-by-10 array.

KeyConcepts.Title: Human evidence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Teacher-observed construction and explanation are part of the lesson, not optional substitutes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not auto-credit a correct total when the source requests a physical array and reasoning.
KeyConcepts.Example: The response '24' alone does not prove any 24-cube arrangement.

WorkedExamples.Title: Twelve eggs: notice and wonder
WorkedExamples.Question: An open carton has 12 eggs. How could equal rows or columns help interpret the arrangement?
WorkedExamples.Method: Look at the source illustration and let learners describe observed rows and columns.
Steps: Look for a repeated arrangement instead of an unordered collection.
Discuss which rows or columns have equal numbers.
Explain an observed grouping to a partner; teacher checks it against the actual original image.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Several valid observations are possible; the actual source image and oral explanation require teacher judgment.
WorkedExamples.Check: Never infer a specific row orientation without showing the original carton source visual.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four circles of five versus an array
WorkedExamples.Question: Can 20 dots in a rectangular array show equal groups as well as four circles of five?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare a set of equal groups with one rectangular organization.
Steps: Rearrange the same 20 objects into 4 equal rows of 5.
Check that each row has five and each column has four.
Explain why Noah's assertion that arrays have no equal groups is incorrect.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes; rows and columns of an array form equal groups.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks diagram construction and argument.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build six groups of five
WorkedExamples.Question: Show an array using 30 connecting cubes.
WorkedExamples.Method: First physically make six equal groups of five, then place them in equal-length rows.
Steps: Make six groups with five cubes in each.
Arrange six rows of five cubes.
Check five columns each of six cubes.
Explain why there are still 30 objects.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A 6-by-5 array of 30 cubes is a valid original Edulytics example.
WorkedExamples.Check: Student's own cube arrangement and explanation require teacher review.

WorkedExamples.Title: Make different arrays of twenty and twenty-four
WorkedExamples.Question: Find different rectangular organizations without changing the total number of cubes.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use all cubes and check row/column equality.
Steps: For 20 cubes, demonstrate 4 rows of 5 and 2 rows of 10.
For 24 cubes, demonstrate 4 rows of 6 and 3 rows of 8.
Discuss which rows and columns count as equal groups.
A teacher verifies each created drawing; exhaustive factor-pair enumeration is not required.
WorkedExamples.Answer: More than one valid array for each total, with geometrically regular rows/columns.
WorkedExamples.Check: Multiple correct configurations exist; teacher marks constructions, not only counts.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a rectangle-shaped arrangement cannot show equal groups.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Both the equal-length rows and the equal-length columns are groups of the same size.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Inspect four groups of five and a corresponding 4-by-5 array.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Awarding source array success because the number 30, 20 or 24 is correct.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The lesson asks children to build, compare and explain physical arrays.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep original source tasks and first-party Cool-down teacher-reviewed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Requiring all possible arrays for 24 cubes.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 2021 teacher narrative explicitly says exhaustive enumeration is NOT a Grade 3 expectation here.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Accept several valid arrays with reasoning; do not demand every factor pair.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Copying source photographs or artwork into first-party teaching.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original media rights and geometry are not certified for reuse.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use teacher-authorized originals when needed or first-party diagrams with clear provenance.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up: teacher-led Notice and Wonder using the source 12-egg carton image.
Activity 1: both four circles of five and a 20-dot rectangular array show equal groups; children critique Noah with reasoning.
Activity 2: each pair receives at least 60 cubes; first construct six groups of five, then arrays with all 20 and with all 24 cubes.
Different valid rows-by-columns forms are allowed. Exhaustively listing arrays is not a required Grade 3 skill.
Original source drawings, oral discussion and manipulative evidence are human-judged and must never be replaced by generic integer questions.
First-party additional array task and Cool-down are teacher-reviewed, not numeric pass/fail.
